analysis.one_liner: Bans leaded aviation fuel from all flights in U.S. airspace starting in 2021.
analysis.headline: The bill to ban leaded aircraft fuel was introduced in March 2016 and died in a House subcommittee without ever getting a vote.
analysis.plain_summary: Piston-engine small aircraft still burn leaded gasoline, the only remaining use of leaded fuel in the United States. This bill would have directed the Federal Aviation Administration, working with the EPA, to write rules banning leaded fuel in all aircraft flying in U.S. airspace starting January 1, 2021. It was sent to the House Transportation and Infrastructure Committee and its Aviation subcommittee, where it stayed until Congress ended.
analysis.who_benefits: People who live, work, or go to school near small airports, where lead from aircraft exhaust settles into soil and air, and children especially, since lead exposure harms brain development at any level. It also benefits pilots and airport workers who breathe aviation fuel fumes regularly.

how_it_helps.text: It would end the last lawful use of leaded fuel in the United States by requiring the FAA to prohibit leaded fuel in all aircraft in U.S. airspace beginning January 1, 2021 [S2][S3].
The FAA would have to write the rules in consultation with the EPA, the agency responsible for air-quality standards [S3].

analysis.who_pays: Owners and operators of piston-engine aircraft, which would need engines certified for unleaded fuel, and the fuel suppliers and refiners who make leaded aviation gasoline. Some costs could pass through to flying schools and small-plane users through higher fuel and aircraft prices.

drawbacks.text: A January 2021 deadline gave aircraft makers and fuel producers under five years to develop and certify a drop-in unleaded fuel, which industry groups argued could ground some planes or raise costs for flying schools and small operators; no such timeline argument appears in the record, so this reflects how the mechanism works generally.
The bill simply ordered a prohibition without funding or a transition program, so any compliance cost would fall directly on general aviation without assistance.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: Ending lead exposure, especially for children near airports, is a substantial public-health gain, and leaded aviation fuel was already the last leaded gasoline use in the country. The honest cost is that small piston aircraft needed a certified unleaded fuel to keep flying, and a hard deadline with no transition assistance risked raising costs for flying schools, crop dusters, and small-plane owners. A phased mandate with transition support would have balanced the two better, but the bill contained no such support.

outcome.mechanism: It was referred to the House Transportation and Infrastructure Committee and then to its Aviation subcommittee, and that is where it stayed until Congress ended; no committee vote, no floor vote, nothing further.

narrative.text: Del. Eleanor Holmes Norton introduced the bill on March 2, 2016, and it was referred the same day to the House Committee on Transportation and Infrastructure [S1][S5].
The next day it was sent to the subcommittee on Aviation, and no further action was ever recorded before the 114th Congress ended on January 3, 2017 [S5].
The bill attracted one cosponsor, Rep. Steve Cohen, a Democrat, and no Republicans [S4].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Operators and fuel suppliers who continued selling and burning leaded aviation gasoline without facing a phase-out deadline, while residents near small airports kept absorbing the lead exposure the bill would have ended.

for.name: Del. Eleanor Holmes Norton
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and spoke for it on the House floor record.

for.name: Rep. Steve Cohen
for.what_they_did: Signed on as the bill's only cosponsor.

against.name: House Transportation and Infrastructure Committee
against.role: Committee of referral, chaired by Rep. Bill Shuster (R)
against.what_they_did: Never took the bill up; it was referred to the committee on March 2, 2016, and never reported out.

against.name: Aviation Subcommittee
against.what_they_did: Received the bill on March 3, 2016, and held no action on it for the rest of the Congress.

sides.party_line_note: The bill had only two Democratic sponsors and no Republican support in the record, and it never advanced far enough for anyone to vote on it, so no party split was ever tested.

industries.industry: General aviation (piston-engine aircraft owners, flying schools, operators)
industries.note: These operators would have had to fly on certified unleaded fuel by 2021 or retrofit their aircraft, raising their operating costs. Their continued use of leaded fuel is precisely what exposed people near airports to lead.
Producers of leaded aviation gasoline would have lost their market when the ban took effect. They had a stake in delaying or weakening any phase-out.
